Rule.fixtext: Enable Network Policy enforcement for EKS Auto Mode by applying or updating the amazon-vpc-cni ConfigMap in the kube-system namespace with enable-network- policy-controller: true. There is no separate EKS cluster update command for this setting in Auto Mode. Create a file named enable-network-policy.yaml: apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: amazon-vpc-cni namespace: kube-system data: enable-network-policy-controller: "true" Apply the ConfigMap: kubectl apply -f enable-network-policy.yaml Validate the setting: Internal Only - General kubectl get configmap amazon-vpc-cni -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.enable-network-policy-controller}{"\n"}' • After the controller is enabled, apply the required Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources or supported EKS network policy resources for the workloads that need traffic restrictions. Enabling the controller provides enforcement capability, but it does not create workload ingress or egress policy rules by itself. If required, configure NodeClass network policy behavior separately to set default allow or default deny behavior and enable network policy event logging. EKS Auto Mode supports these settings through NodeClass, while CloudWatch export for network event logs is not supported

check.check-content: Review the EKS Auto Mode Network Policy Controller configuration and verify that Network Policy enforcement is enabled for the cluster. In EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages the VPC CNI configuration, so the audit should not rely on managed add-on version checks, the aws-node DaemonSet, or legacy VPC CNI environment variables. The Auto Mode specific audit is to verify that the amazon-vpc-cni ConfigMap exists in the kube-system namespace and that enable-network-policy-controller is set to true. Use this command to check whether the Network Policy Controller is enabled: kubectl get configmap amazon-vpc-cni -n kube-system \ -o jsonpath='{.data.enable-network-policy-controller}' 2>/dev/null • The expected value is true. If the command returns not-set or the ConfigMap is not found, Network Policy enforcement has not been enabled for EKS Auto Mode. In addition, review the NodeClass network policy settings because EKS Auto Mode can use NodeClass to configure network policy behavior, including default allow, default deny, and network policy event logging. kubectl get nodeclass -o custom- columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NETWORK_POLICY:.spec.networkPolicy,EVENT_LOGS:.sp ec.networkPolicyEventLogs • This confirms whether any Auto Mode NodeClass resources define network policy behavior that affects the nodes using that class.

Rule.title: Restrict workload traffic with Kubernetes Network Policies
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>EKS Auto Mode supports Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources for namespace Layer 3 and Layer 4 pod traffic isolation, and also supports broader EKS network policy capabilities such as ClusterNetworkPolicy and ApplicationNetworkPolicy where applicable. Workload isolation depends on the relevant workloads actually being covered by NetworkPolicy, ClusterNetworkPolicy, or other supported EKS network policy resources. NetworkPolicy provides namespace pod traffic segmentation, while ClusterNetworkPolicy can apply a common security posture across all or a selected subset of workloads in the cluster.
Rationale: Enabling the EKS Auto Mode Network Policy Controller only provides the enforcement capability. Traffic restrictions are not realized unless policies are defined for the workloads, namespaces, or cluster scopes that need them. Standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources control traffic at Network and Transport layers, while ClusterNetworkPolicy can centralize controls across the cluster or selected namespaces. A least privilege approach should start with restrictive policies, such as deny by default controls, and then add explicit ingress and egress allow rules for required application flows. EKS evaluates Admin tier ClusterNetworkPolicy rules first, then namespace policies such as NetworkPolicy and ApplicationNetworkPolicy, then baseline policies, and finally deny by default behavior when no policies match.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Create and apply Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, ApplicationNetworkPolicy, or ClusterNetworkPolicy objects so every required workload is explicitly covered by policy. Use namespace NetworkPolicy for workload Network and Transport layer segmentation, use ApplicationNetworkPolicy when DNS egress filtering is required, and use ClusterNetworkPolicy when a shared security posture must apply across multiple namespaces or workload groups. EKS Auto Mode supports these network policy patterns for pod traffic isolation and centralized network access controls. • Set default deny and then add only the ingress and egress rules needed for approved traffic such as DNS, required service-to-service flows, and authorized external destinations. Use specific selectors and destinations rather than broad namespace, pod, IP, or domain patterns whenever possible. • If the policy uses DNS rules through ApplicationNetworkPolicy, schedule the affected workloads on EKS Auto Mode EC2 instances and validate that required DNS resolution and egress traffic still function as expected. DNS rules in ApplicationNetworkPolicy apply only to workloads running on EKS Auto Mode EC2 instances. • For shared cluster controls, define ClusterNetworkPolicy with the appropriate tier, priority, subject selectors, and action. Use Admin tier deny rules for controls that namespace teams should not be able to override, and use Pass or namespace policies where teams should manage lower level application traffic. After applying or updating policies, validate allowed and denied traffic paths with representative workloads.

check.check-content: Review the Kubernetes network policy in the EKS Auto Mode cluster and verify that every required workload is selected by either namespace NetworkPolicy, ApplicationNetworkPolicy, or a cluster ClusterNetworkPolicy. A separate policy in every namespace is not always required because ClusterNetworkPolicy can apply shared controls across all workloads or selected namespaces, while namespace policies can provide application segmentation. EKS Auto Mode supports different network policy types, including standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, DNS-based policies, and cluster rules. Confirm that Network Policy enforcement is set to true before reviewing policy coverage. kubectl get configmap amazon-vpc-cni -n kube-system \ -o jsonpath='{.data.enable-network-policy-controller}{"\n"}' 2>/dev/null Identify all policy objects intended to govern workload traffic: kubectl get networkpolicy -A kubectl get applicationnetworkpolicy -A kubectl get clusternetworkpolicy • Map each required workload to the policy or policies that select it, and confirm no required workload falls outside policy coverage. Review podSelector, namespaceSelector, policy tiers, and ingress and egress rules to confirm that policies match the intended pods, namespaces, ports, protocols, and approved destinations. EKS evaluates Admin tier ClusterNetworkPolicy first, then namespace ApplicationNetworkPolicy and NetworkPolicy, then baseline policies, and finally default deny behavior when no policies match. • Review selectors and ingress and egress rules to confirm least privilege design. A strong pattern is to start with restrictive or deny by default policies, then add explicit allow rules for required flows such as DNS, approved service-to-service traffic, and authorized external endpoints. • Confirm that DNS-based policy rules are only used for workloads running on EKS Auto Mode-launched EC2 instances. In mixed-mode clusters, verify that workloads requiring DNS enforcement are scheduled onto Auto Mode nodes. • Review standalone or unmanaged pods separately because AWS documents network policy coverage considerations for pods that are not part of a Deployment. Do not assume that the existence of policy objects means every workload is governed. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Mount secrets as files instead of environment variables
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Secrets for EKS workloads are better exposed as mounted files than as environment variables. Kubernetes Secrets can be consumed either way, and AWS supports file delivery from AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store through the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver. In EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages more of the underlying cluster infrastructure, but customers remain responsible for the security of the application containers and pods that consume secrets.
Rationale: Environment variable values can unintentionally appear in logs, while secrets mounted as volumes are instantiated as tmpfs volumes and are automatically removed from the node when the pod is deleted. Mounting secrets as files reduces accidental exposure through application logs, process inspection patterns, and configuration dumps that commonly include environment variables. File delivery also aligns with the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider (ASCP) best practice, which mounts Secrets Manager and Parameter Store values into EKS Pods as files. With ASCP, access is controlled through pod identity or IAM roles for service accounts, and the SecretProviderClass defines which secrets are mounted and the file names used inside the pod.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Update workloads to consume secrets as mounted files instead of environment variables. Replace env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef and envFrom[].secretRef usage with Kubernetes Secret volumes or the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, and then update the application to read the secret from the mounted file path. This reduces the chance of secret values appearing in logs and aligns with the recommended file delivery pattern for EKS workloads. For Kubernetes Secrets, mount the Secret as a volume and update the application configuration to read from the mounted path rather than from environment variables. volumes: - name: app-secret secret: secretName: app-secret containers: - name: app volumeMounts: - name: app-secret mountPath: /etc/secrets readOnly: true • For secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, use the Secrets Store CSI Driver with ASCP to mount the values as files in the pod. Use EKS Pod Identity or IRSA to scope access to only the secrets required by that workload, and define the mounted objects and file names in a namespace SecretProviderClass. After the change, redeploy the affected workloads and verify the application reads secrets from the mounted file path. Include file permissions, mount paths, application reload behavior, and rotation handling in validation because mounted files and environment variables behave differently at runtime.

check.check-content: Review workload manifests and identify any Pod, Deployment, DaemonSet, StatefulSet, Job, or CronJob that exposes secrets through environment variables instead of mounted files. Check for both direct secret references through env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef and bulk secret imports through envFrom[].secretRef, because either pattern exposes secret data as environment variables. Prefer workloads that consume secrets through mounted Secret volumes or file delivery from AWS secrets integrations instead. EKS Auto Mode manages more of the underlying infrastructure, but customers remain responsible for how application pods consume secrets. EKS secret management guidance recommends volume mounts instead of environment variables because environment variable values can unintentionally appear in logs, while mounted secret volumes use tmpfs and are removed when the pod is deleted. Run this command to list workloads that reference secrets through either environment variable pattern: kubectl get pod,deploy,ds,sts,job,cronjob -A -o json | jq -r ' .items[] | select([.. | objects | (.env[]?.valueFrom.secretKeyRef?, .envFrom[]?.secretRef?)] | any) | "\(.metadata.namespace)\t\(.kind)/\(.metadata.name)" ' • This command checks pod specs and controller pod templates for secret values exposed through secretKeyRef or secretRef. Any output should be reviewed as a finding unless there is a documented exception. No output means the reviewed workloads are not referencing Kubernetes Secrets through environment variables. Where external secrets are used, also review SecretProviderClass resources to confirm secrets are mounted as files through the Secrets Store CSI Driver and AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider. ASCP can mount Secrets Manager secrets and Parameter Store parameters as files in EKS pods, and the SecretProviderClass defines which secrets are mounted and the file names used inside the pod. kubectl get secretproviderclass -A • Note: If this command returns the server doesn't have a resource type "secretproviderclass", the Secrets Store CSI Driver CRD is not installed in the cluster. In that case, the audit should focus on Kubernetes Secret volume mounts unless the cluster is expected to use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store through ASCP. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Use external secret storage for sensitive values
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Use external secret storage to manage sensitive application values in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store instead of relying only on native Kubernetes Secret objects. This approach lets EKS workloads consume secrets through integrations such as the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, while keeping secret lifecycle functions outside the cluster.
Rationale: Storing high value credentials outside Kubernetes reduces dependence on cluster Secret objects and shifts lifecycle functions such as encryption, access control, rotation, and audit to a dedicated secrets service. In EKS, Pods can retrieve secrets from Secrets Manager by using IAM access through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA, and the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider can mount those values into Pods as files through the Secrets Store CSI Driver. This supports more granular secret to workload access control and reduces the need to distribute static secret values through Kubernetes manifests. This is also better aligned to rotation and centralized governance because Kubernetes does not automatically rotate secrets. External secret stores such as AWS Secrets Manager provide dedicated secret lifecycle management, while EKS workloads can retrieve only the values authorized for their workload identity.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Use AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store as the primary store for application secrets. Update EKS workloads to retrieve those values through the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, using IAM through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA. This shifts encryption, access control, rotation, and auditing to AWS rather than leaving those functions primarily in cluster Secret objects. Internal Only - General • Create the required secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and define least privilege IAM permissions so each workload identity can read only the specific secrets it requires. • Install and configure the Secrets Store CSI Driver and AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider if they are not already present. • Update workloads to mount external secrets through a namespace SecretProviderClass, and configure the application to read secrets from the mounted file path. • Use EKS Pod Identity where possible for Auto Mode workloads, or IRSA where that is the established access model. • Enable rotation, mount paths, file permissions, application reload behavior, and any CSI sync behavior that may create Kubernetes Secret objects.

check.check-content: Audit the EKS Auto Mode cluster’s secrets architecture and verify that required workloads use an external secrets store such as AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store instead of relying only on Kubernetes Secret objects. The audit should confirm both the integration path and the workload access model, because external secret storage in EKS commonly uses the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, plus pod IAM through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA. EKS Auto Mode integrates with EKS Pod Identity, while ASCP can retrieve Secrets Manager secrets or Parameter Store parameters for authorized workloads. Internal Only - General Identify Kubernetes Secrets that may need to move to an external store. kubectl get secrets -A • Identify workloads that consume Kubernetes Secrets through environment variables or mounted Kubernetes Secret volumes. These workloads should be reviewed to determine whether the secret should remain as a Kubernetes Secret or be moved to Secrets Manager or Parameter Store. kubectl get pod,deploy,ds,sts,job,cronjob -A -o json | jq -r ' .items[] | select([.. | objects | (.env[]?.valueFrom.secretKeyRef?, .envFrom[]?.secretRef?, .volumes[]?.secret?)] | any) | "\(.metadata.namespace)\t\(.kind)/\(.metadata.name)" ' • Confirm whether the Secrets Store CSI Driver integration is present by checking for SecretProviderClass resources. If the resource type does not exist, the cluster is not currently using the Secrets Store CSI Driver pattern for external secret mounts. kubectl get secretproviderclass -A 2>/dev/null • Where SecretProviderClass resources exist, review them to confirm they reference the intended Secrets Manager secrets or Parameter Store parameters, mount values as files, and use workload specific access. kubectl get secretproviderclass -A -o yaml • Verify pod access is scoped through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA so each workload can retrieve only the secrets it is authorized to read. ASCP assumes the pod’s authorized IAM role and retrieves only the secrets permitted for that role. • Note: If SecretProviderClass is not recognized and returns error: the server doesn't have a resource type "secretproviderclass", then the Secrets Store CSI Driver CRD is not installed, and the cluster is not using the SecretProviderClass pattern to mount external secrets from AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.

Rule.title: Use dedicated namespaces to separate workload boundaries
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Namespaces create administrative boundaries in EKS by dividing a cluster into logical partitions for teams, applications, environments, or tenants. They are a core building block for soft multitenancy, and several controls used to separate workloads, including quotas, network policies, and service accounts, are defined to the namespace. In EKS Auto Mode, namespaces remain the primary Kubernetes boundary for organizing workload governance even though AWS manages more of the underlying compute, networking, and storage infrastructure.
Rationale: Namespaces matter because many access and governance controls in Kubernetes and EKS can be applied at that level. Kubernetes Roles and RoleBindings delegate permissions within a namespace, and EKS access policies can be one or more specific namespaces instead of the entire cluster. This allows platform administrators to grant access only to the namespaces that a group or workload owner is responsible for, rather than granting cluster permissions. In EKS Auto Mode, this remains important because customers are still responsible for application containers, workload access, and namespace governance. The namespace boundary becomes stronger when paired with additional controls. ResourceQuota and LimitRange can constrain CPU, memory, and object consumption, while NetworkPolicy resources can restrict pod-to-pod communication and support least privilege traffic controls between tenant or application namespaces. A namespace alone is only a logical grouping, so effective separation depends on pairing it with RBAC, access scoping, quotas, service accounts, and network isolation.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Create dedicated namespaces for groups, applications, or environments that need separate administrative scope, and move workloads out of the default namespace. Strengthen each namespace boundary with targeted access, quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies, and reduce cluster permissions that bypass the intended separation model. EKS Auto Mode manages more of the data plane infrastructure, but namespace design, workload placement, access control, and application governance remain customer responsibilities. Create dedicated namespaces for each group, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary. kubectl create namespace $NAMESPACE • Move user workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate managed namespace. • Rebind access with namespace Role and RoleBinding objects and, where used, scope EKS access policies to one or more specific namespaces instead of the whole cluster. AmazonEKSAdminPolicy is typically one or more namespaces, while AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy grants administrator access to the cluster. • Apply ResourceQuota, LimitRange, dedicated service accounts, and network policies to reinforce namespace governance and traffic separation. • Remove unused namespaces and reduce unnecessary ClusterRoleBinding, cluster access policy, or access entry assignments that bypass the intended namespace boundary. When stronger isolation is required for mutually untrusted workloads, use separate clusters or stronger isolation patterns rather than relying on namespaces alone. AWS states that namespace based soft multitenancy provides logical separation, while the cluster is the stronger security boundary.

check.check-content: Verify that namespaces are being used as intentional administrative boundaries for groups, applications, or environments in the EKS Auto Mode cluster. Namespaces should be paired with scoped access controls and namespace governance such as quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies. In EKS Auto Mode, customers remain responsible for application containers, workload access, and namespace governance even though AWS manages more of the underlying infrastructure. • Confirm that namespaces have a defined administrative, application, or environment purpose, and verify that access is scoped through namespace Role and RoleBinding objects instead of unnecessary cluster ClusterRole or ClusterRoleBinding. • Review EKS access entries and associated access policies to confirm IAM principals are scoped to specific namespaces where appropriate. EKS access policies can be scoped to specific Kubernetes namespaces or to the entire cluster. aws eks list-access-entries \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --output json aws eks list-associated-access-policies \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --principal-arn $PRINCIPAL_ARN \ --query 'associatedAccessPolicies[].{Policy:policyArn,Scope:accessScope}' \ --output json • Review whether namespace controls such as ResourceQuota, LimitRange, service accounts, and network policies are applied where required to support separation, resource governance, and east/west traffic restrictions. kubectl get resourcequota,limitrange,networkpolicy -A kubectl get serviceaccounts -A • Confirm that cluster access is limited to identities that truly require it, because namespaces provide logical separation but do not create a strong security boundary by themselves. Use separate clusters or stronger isolation patterns when workloads are mutually untrusted. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Avoid deploying workloads in the default namespace
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Avoid placing application workloads in the default namespace, and instead deploy them into dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended group, application, environment, or tenant boundary. In EKS, namespaces are the primary logical partition for organizing workloads and supporting soft multitenancy in a shared cluster. In EKS Auto Mode, this remains important because AWS manages more of the underlying infrastructure, but customers still manage workload placement, access control, and application governance.
Rationale: Least privilege administration in EKS depends on using namespaces as intentional boundaries. Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding objects apply within namespaces, and EKS access policies can be limited to one or more specific namespaces instead of the whole cluster. When workloads remain in default, access delegation, ownership boundaries, and namespace based governance become harder to separate cleanly. Dedicated namespaces also make it easier to apply supporting controls such as ResourceQuota, LimitRange, service accounts, and network policies to the correct workloads. EKS tenant isolation guidance describes namespaces, RBAC, quotas, limit ranges, and network policies used to create logical separation, while EKS Auto Mode network policy capabilities can isolate tenants at the namespace.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Move user workloads out of the default namespace and place them in dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended group, application, or environment boundary. In EKS, namespaces are the core logical partition for soft multi-tenancy, but they only become meaningful administrative boundaries when paired with access controls, service accounts, quotas, limits, and network policies. EKS Auto Mode manages infrastructure components such as compute, pod and service networking, load balancing, DNS, and storage, but workload placement and namespace governance remain customer responsibilities. • Create dedicated namespaces for each group, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary. • Redeploy or migrate user workloads from default into the appropriate dedicated namespace. • Update manifests, Helm values, GitOps definitions, and pipeline defaults so namespaced resources explicitly set metadata.namespace and are not created in default by omission. • Rework access with namespace based Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding objects and, where EKS access entries are used, associate EKS access policies to specific namespaces instead of the whole cluster. • Apply namespace governance such as ResourceQuota, LimitRange, dedicated service accounts, and network policies so the namespace boundary supports resource control, identity separation, and east west traffic isolation. • Remove unnecessary user workloads and broad operational access from default, and use separate clusters rather than namespaces alone when stronger isolation is required for less trusted workloads.

check.check-content: Review the EKS Auto Mode cluster and verify that the default namespace is not being used for routine application workload placement. Objects that do not explicitly specify a namespace are created in default, so the audit should confirm that groups, applications, and environments use dedicated namespaces aligned to access control, quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies. AWS identifies namespaces as a fundamental construct for soft multi-tenancy, with quotas, network policies, service accounts, and related objects used to support logical separation. Inventory the default namespace and identify user managed Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, ServiceAccounts, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs, Ingresses, Roles, RoleBindings, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, or NetworkPolicies that still exist there. kubectl get pod,svc,configmap,secret,serviceaccount,deploy,statefulset,daemonset,job,cron job,ingress,role,rolebinding,resourcequota,limitrange,networkpolicy -n default • Review whether any application workloads, application secrets, application ConfigMaps, custom service accounts, or workload access bindings remain in default. System generated or temporary objects should be reviewed separately from normal application resources. • Verify that access is not centered on default. Review Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding assignments for that namespace and, where EKS access entries are used, confirm that access policies are limited to the intended namespaces rather than applied across the entire cluster. EKS access policies support both namespace limited access and cluster wide access. • Confirm that user workloads are placed into dedicated namespaces that reflect group, application, or environment boundaries, and that namespace controls such as quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies are applied where required. These controls make the namespace an administrative boundary instead of only a naming container. Check whether the namespace design reduces shared administration and naming sprawl. AWS describes namespaces as logical partitions for soft multi-tenancy, while also noting that the cluster is the only strong security boundary. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Enable ECR enhanced scanning for EKS Auto Mode workload images
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Container image vulnerability scanning helps strengthen the security of EKS Auto Mode workload images by identifying known software weaknesses before or after images are deployed. Because EKS Auto Mode manages more of the cluster infrastructure while customers remain responsible for application containers and pods, image scanning remains a customer controlled workload security requirement.
Rationale: ECR enhanced scanning integrates with Amazon Inspector to provide automated and continuous vulnerability scanning for container images stored in Amazon ECR. Unlike basic scanning, enhanced scanning includes both operating system and programming language package vulnerabilities, updates findings as new CVEs are identified, and can emit events through EventBridge when findings are created, updated, or closed. This is especially important for EKS Auto Mode because customer responsibility remains focused on the workloads they deploy, even though the underlying managed instances and several cluster infrastructure capabilities are handled by EKS Auto Mode. ECR enhanced scanning can also show image usage in EKS, including when images were last used and how many clusters use each image, which helps prioritize remediation for vulnerable images that are actually running. Images with High or Critical findings should be rebuilt, replaced, or removed based on risk and operational requirements.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Enable ECR enhanced scanning for the private registry in each Region that stores images used by EKS Auto Mode workloads. Use registry scanning configuration rather than repository scan on push configuration, because the repository PutImageScanningConfiguration API is being deprecated in favor of registry configuration. Enhanced scanning integrates ECR with Amazon Inspector to provide automated and continuous scanning for operating system and programming language package vulnerabilities. Identify the ECR repositories and Regions that provide images to EKS Auto Mode workloads. Use the image references from Kubernetes workloads to determine which ECR repositories must be covered by enhanced scanning. Enable enhanced scanning for the private registry in each applicable Region. When no rules are specified, ECR sets enhanced scanning to continuous scanning for all repositories by default. Internal Only - General aws ecr put-registry-scanning-configuration \ --scan-type ENHANCED \ --region $REGION_CODE • If your organization uses repository filters, configure rules so all repositories that supply EKS Auto Mode workload images are included. The following example continuously scans repositories with prod in the repository name. aws ecr put-registry-scanning-configuration \ --scan-type ENHANCED \ --rules '[{"repositoryFilters":[{"filter":"prod","filterType":"WILDCARD"}],"scanFrequ ency":"CONTINUOUS_SCAN"}]' \ --region $REGION_CODE • For broader coverage, use a wildcard rule to continuously scan all repositories that may supply EKS Auto Mode workloads. aws ecr put-registry-scanning-configuration \ --scan-type ENHANCED \ --rules '[{"repositoryFilters":[{"filter":"*","filterType":"WILDCARD"}],"scanFrequenc y":"CONTINUOUS_SCAN"}]' \ --region $REGION_CODE • After enabling enhanced scanning, review Amazon Inspector findings, prioritize High and Critical vulnerabilities, rebuild or replace affected images, and redeploy updated workload images to the EKS Auto Mode cluster. This makes scanning part of the operational deployment control path rather than only a reporting activity. ECR enhanced scanning also sends EventBridge events when findings are created, updated, or closed, which can support alerting and remediation workflows.

check.check-content: Verify that ECR enhanced scanning is enabled for repositories that store images used by EKS Auto Mode workloads. EKS Auto Mode manages more of the cluster infrastructure, but customers remain responsible for the security, availability, and monitoring of the containers and pods they deploy. Internal Only - General Review the ECR registry scanning configuration in each Region that stores images for the cluster. Confirm that scanType is ENHANCED and that the configured rules include the repositories used by EKS Auto Mode workloads. The registry scanning configuration defines the registry scan type, repository filters, and scan frequency. aws ecr get-registry-scanning-configuration \ --region $REGION_CODE Expected output: JSON showing registryId and scanningConfiguration. In scanningConfiguration, look for scanType: ENHANCED and review rules, repositoryFilters, and scanFrequency. For this control, repositories used by EKS Auto Mode workloads should be covered by CONTINUOUS_SCAN unless there is a documented reason to use SCAN_ON_PUSH. Check the effective scanning configuration for each repository used by EKS Auto Mode workload images. This confirms whether the repository is actually covered by the registry scanning rules and which filters apply. aws ecr batch-get-repository-scanning-configuration \ --repository-names $REPO_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE Expected output: JSON with scanningConfigurations for the requested repository. Review repositoryName, repositoryArn, scanFrequency, and appliedScanFilters. A repository covered by enhanced continuous scanning should show scanFrequency as CONTINUOUS_SCAN. Repositories that do not match enhanced scanning filters may not be scanned, so they should be treated as audit findings for this control. Review ECR or Amazon Inspector findings for repositories that supply EKS Auto Mode workload images. Confirm that High and Critical findings are reviewed, tracked, and remediated through image rebuild, replacement, or removal before the affected images are promoted or continue running in production.

Rule.title: Enforce least privilege for ECR repositories storing EKS Auto Mode workload images
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Least privilege access for Amazon ECR repositories helps limit who can pull, push, delete, or administer container images used by EKS Auto Mode workloads. This reduces unnecessary exposure of the image registry and helps ensure that only the identities required to support image pulls, image publishing, release promotion, and repository administration can access the repositories. EKS Auto Mode shifts more infrastructure management to AWS.
Rationale: Amazon ECR access is enforced through a combination of IAM identity based policies and ECR repository policies. IAM policies can grant ECR permissions across the service or to specific resources, while repository policies are applied directly to individual repositories. For EKS Auto Mode workload image pulls, runtime identities should be limited to pull only actions needed to authenticate to ECR and retrieve image layers, such as ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchGetImage, ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer, and ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability. For image push, repository administration, deletion, replication, or cross account access, permissions should be separated by role and limited to the specific repository ARNs, actions, principals, and conditions required for the use case. This aligns with AWS IAM least privilege practices and reduces the risk that a node role, workload identity, CI/CD role, or operator account can modify, overwrite, delete, or access images beyond its operational need.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Enforce least privilege access for ECR repositories used by EKS Auto Mode workload images by separating image pull, image push, account access, and repository administration into different IAM roles and policy scopes. Grant the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role only the ECR permissions needed to authenticate and pull images, such as ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability, ecr:BatchGetImage, and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer. Scope CI/CD and administrator access to the specific repositories and actions they require, and review both IAM identity based policies and ECR repository policies because ECR authorization can be affected by both. Separate ECR access by role. Use different roles for EKS Auto Mode runtime image pulls, CI/CD image pushes, account repository access, and repository administration. • Replace broad pull access with pull-only permissions where possible. Attach a narrower pull-only policy to runtime pull roles instead of broader ECR access. For EKS Auto Mode node roles, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly is the managed policy AWS identifies for ECR image pull access. aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name $ROLE_NAME \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly • Scope push and admin access to specific repositories. Limit CI/CD and admin identities to the repository ARNs and ECR actions they actually need. Use customer policies where the managed policy grants more access than the specific build, release, or administration function requires. • Tighten repository policies only where needed. Use repository policies to restrict repository access, including approved account access, but remember that ecr:GetAuthorizationToken must still come from IAM. Internal Only - General aws ecr set-repository-policy \ --repository-name $REPO_NAME \ --policy-text file://repo-policy.json \ --region $REGION_CODE • Keep runtime pull roles limited to pull actions only. Do not give EKS Auto Mode Node IAM roles push, delete, replication, lifecycle, or policy-management rights unless there is a documented operational requirement. Remove broad ECR managed policies such as full access or power user from runtime pull roles when pull-only access is sufficient. Retest image delivery after policy changes. Confirm EKS Auto Mode workloads can still pull required images and that unauthorized identities can no longer push, delete, or administer repositories outside their approved role.

check.check-content: Review the IAM permissions and ECR repository policies that apply to repositories used by EKS Auto Mode workload images, and verify that access is limited to approved EKS Auto Mode Node IAM roles, CI/CD identities, cross-account principals, and repository administration roles. Confirm that runtime pull access is limited to the minimum ECR actions required for image retrieval, that push or administrative access is limited to the repositories and actions required, and that no unnecessary wildcard or broad cross- account access is present. ECR access decisions can be affected by both IAM policies and repository policies, and EKS Auto Mode uses a Node IAM role whose key permissions include pulling images from ECR. Review each repository policy for unnecessary principals or broad actions. Look for cross-account access, wildcard principals, or actions beyond the repository’s intended use. ECR repository policies are used to control access to individual private repositories, but ecr:GetAuthorizationToken must still be granted through IAM before a principal can authenticate to push or pull images. aws ecr get-repository-policy \ --repository-name $REPO_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE • Expected output: JSON containing the repository policy text. Review the Principal, Action, and Resource entries to confirm access is limited to approved identities and required actions only. Flag wildcard principals, broad cross account access, unrestricted push access, delete permissions, or policy permissions that are not required for the repository’s intended use. Review the IAM role used to pull images. For EKS Auto Mode workloads, review the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role, commonly named AmazonEKSAutoNodeRole. If the cluster also uses Fargate profiles, review the Fargate pod execution role separately. Confirm the role has only the pull permissions required for ECR access. Pull related permissions include ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability, ecr:BatchGetImage, and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer. aws iam list-attached-role-policies \ --role-name $ROLE_NAME • Expected output: JSON listing the managed policies attached to the role. Review the attached policy names and flag overly broad access such as full ECR administration where pull-only access would be sufficient. For EKS Auto Mode node roles, confirm that pull access is satisfied through AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly or an equivalent customer policy with only the required pull actions. Also review inline policies attached directly to the role, because broad ECR permissions may be granted outside managed policies. Internal Only - General aws iam list-role-policies \ --role-name $ROLE_NAME • Expected output: JSON listing inline policy names attached to the role. If inline policies are present, retrieve and review them for broad permissions such as ecr:*, wildcard repository resources, push actions, delete actions, or repository policy actions assigned to runtime pull roles. Flag broad access patterns. Examples include ecr:*, wildcard repository scope where it is not required, broad managed policies where a narrower customer policy would satisfy the use case, or repository policies that allow unapproved principals. IAM best practices for ECR call for moving from broad managed permissions toward least privilege customer policies that grant only the actions, resources, and conditions required for the use case.

Rule.title: Restrict EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role to ECR pull-only permissions
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Restricting ECR access for the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role to pull only permissions helps ensure that nodes can retrieve required container images without receiving broader registry visibility, image publishing, deletion, or administrative access. In EKS Auto Mode, the Node IAM role is assigned to nodes created for pending workloads and should be used for node operations such as image pulls, not as a broad workload or registry administration identity.
Rationale: The EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role should only have the ECR permissions required to authenticate to ECR and retrieve container image layers. EKS Auto Mode node role setup includes AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly, or equivalent permissions, along with the required EKS node permissions. This keeps node image pull access aligned to the runtime need without granting image push, delete, repository policy, or registry administration permissions. A pull only policy is narrower than ECR read only or broader ECR managed policies. AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly grants permission to pull container images from ECR, while AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly also includes the ability to list repositories and images. Those additional visibility permissions may be useful for administrators, auditors, or tooling, but they are not required for the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role to pull private ECR images.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Enforce pull-only ECR access for the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role by limiting the role to the permissions required to authenticate to ECR and retrieve container image layers. The EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role should use AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly or equivalent permissions, together with the required EKS node permissions. Identify the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role in scope. Use the role configured in the cluster’s Auto Mode compute configuration or the expected role name, such as AmazonEKSAutoNodeRole. Remove broader ECR managed policies from the Node IAM role. Detach AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryFullAccess, or similar broad policies from the role when it only needs image-pull access. ECR managed policies are general purpose, and customer-managed policies can further reduce permissions for specific use cases. aws iam detach-role-policy \ --role-name $ROLE_NAME \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly • Attach the pull-only managed policy to the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role. AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly is the managed-policy fit for ECR image pulls and is one of the suggested policies for the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role. aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name $ROLE_NAME \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly • Remove or replace inline policies that add extra ECR permissions. Keep the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role limited to the pull path and remove repository listing, repository policy reads, scan finding reads, push actions, delete actions, lifecycle actions, and wildcard ecr:* access unless there is a documented operational need. • Check repository policies for unnecessary grants. Repository policies should not reintroduce broader access for the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role, and ecr:GetAuthorizationToken must still be granted through IAM even when a repository policy is used. Internal Only - General aws ecr set-repository-policy \ --repository-name $REPO_NAME \ --policy-text file://repo-policy.json \ --region $REGION_CODE • Retest image pulls after the change. Confirm that EKS Auto Mode workloads can still pull required private ECR images and that the Node IAM role no longer has broader repository visibility, push, delete, or administrative access than required.

check.check-content: Review the IAM permissions and any ECR repository policies that apply to the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role, and verify that the role is limited to pull-only ECR access. For this control, focus on the Node IAM role assigned to EKS Auto Mode nodes. If the cluster also uses Fargate, review the Fargate pod execution role under a separate Fargate specific check. The EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role has key permissions that include pulling images from ECR, and the suggested node role policies include AmazonEKSWorkerNodeMinimalPolicy and AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly. Identify the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role in scope. Review the role configured for Auto Mode compute, commonly named AmazonEKSAutoNodeRole. aws eks describe-cluster \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --query 'cluster.computeConfig.nodeRoleArn' \ --output text • Expected output: the ARN of the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role. Use the role name from this ARN for the remaining IAM checks. Review the managed policies attached to that role. Flag broad policies such as AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser, or AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryFullAccess when the role only needs to pull images. AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly is the tighter policy fit for runtime image pulls because it grants permission to pull container images from ECR, while AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly also allows repository and image listing. aws iam list-attached-role-policies \ --role-name $ROLE_NAME • Expected output: JSON listing managed policies attached to the role. Confirm that ECR access is provided by AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly or an equivalent customer pull-only policy, and flag broader ECR policies unless there is a documented operational requirement. o Review any inline policies attached to the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role and confirm they do not add broader ECR permissions, such as repository listing, scan finding reads, push, delete, lifecycle, policy management, or wildcard ecr:* access. Check for repository exceptions. If a repository policy is used, verify that it does not grant the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role unnecessary push, delete, policy, or administrative access. A missing repository policy is not automatically a finding, because ECR access can be granted through IAM alone. ecr:GetAuthorizationToken must still be granted through IAM before a principal can authenticate to a registry and push or pull images. Internal Only - General aws ecr get-repository-policy \ --repository-name $REPO_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE • Expected output: JSON containing the repository policy text. Review Principal, Action, and Resource entries to confirm the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role is not granted broader access than image retrieval requires.

Rule.title: Restrict EKS Auto Mode workload images to approved registries
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Restricting EKS Auto Mode workload images to approved registries helps reduce software supply chain risk by ensuring workloads are sourced only from trusted image locations. Approved registry controls provide a workload guardrail that complements image scanning, image signing, and deployment governance.
Rationale: A practical way to enforce this control in EKS Auto Mode is through policy as code admission controls such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper, which evaluate Kubernetes workload requests before they are admitted. EKS Auto Mode nodes remain Kubernetes conformant, so standard Kubernetes policy enforcement tools can be used to limit workload configuration, including container image source rules. Approved registry policies can reject pods or workload controllers that reference images from untrusted registries, while optional signature verification can add a stronger trust check for signed images. For signature verification, EKS supports admission based approaches such as Gatekeeper with Ratify or Kyverno, and requires a Notation trust store and trust policy for the selected admission controller. This turns image origin and publisher trust into an admission time control instead of relying only on naming standards or manual review.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Restrict EKS Auto Mode workload images to approved container registries by enforcing image source controls at admission time, rather than relying only on CI/CD checks or written standards. Enforcement is typically implemented with a policy admission controller such as Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, or another validating admission path so image references are checked before the workload is admitted. EKS Auto Mode supports standard Kubernetes policy enforcement tools, making admission time registry restrictions appropriate for Auto Mode workload governance. Include internal ECR repositories, explicitly approved third-party registries, and required ECR registries for EKS add-ons, platform components, security agents, and operational tooling in the approved registry allowlist. EKS add-on images are pulled from Region- specific ECR private repositories, and some security agents may require their registry to be added to an allowed-container-registries admission policy before deployment or update. • Configure Kyverno, Gatekeeper, or another validating admission path so image registry source is checked before the workload is admitted. The policy should match the registry hostname portion of the image reference and deny images from registries that are not explicitly approved. Internal Only - General • Apply the policy to workload namespaces while accounting for system namespaces and approved operational exceptions so required platform components are not blocked. Use separate exception handling for vendor agents, EKS add-ons, and operational tools rather than weakening the global allowlist. • Configure the admission controller to verify signed images and attested artifacts when stronger supply chain controls are required. Registry allowlisting can stand alone, while signature verification adds publisher and artifact integrity checks. For EKS image verification patterns, configure the required Notation trust store and trust policy for the selected admission controller.

check.check-content: Review the image sources currently used by the cluster and the admission controls that govern new deployments, then verify that EKS Auto Mode workload images are limited to approved registries only. EKS Auto Mode nodes are Kubernetes conformant, so standard Kubernetes policy enforcement tools can be used to limit workload configuration, including allowed image registries. Internal Only - General Compare running workload image registry hostnames to the approved registry allowlist. Any image sourced from an unapproved registry is a finding. Include images from regular containers and init containers so supporting startup images are not missed. kubectl get pods -A \ -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{"\t"}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{range .spec.initContainers[*]}{.image}{" "}{end}{range .spec.containers[*]}{.image}{" "}{end}{"\n"}{end}' • Confirm the cluster uses an admission control path that evaluates image source before deployment is accepted, rather than relying only on CI/CD checks or documented standards. Review the Kyverno, Gatekeeper, or equivalent policy configuration to confirm that unapproved registry hostnames are denied at admission time. • Check the approved registry allowlist. Verify it includes internal ECR repositories, approved third-party registries if any, and required ECR registries for EKS add- ons, platform components, security agents, and operational tooling that are deployed in the cluster. EKS add-on images are pulled from ECR private repositories replicated by Region, so required AWS managed image sources should be included where those add-ons are used. • Confirm an approved image is accepted and a test image from an unapproved registry is rejected at admission time. Perform this validation in a non-production namespace or controlled test namespace to avoid disrupting active workloads. Verify any additional allowed registries are documented and approved.

Rule.title: Use dedicated service accounts for EKS Auto Mode workload identities
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for EKS Auto Mode workload identities helps isolate AWS permissions by application, job, or trust boundary instead of sharing a single identity across multiple workloads. This supports more controlled access to AWS services and reduces the blast radius if one workload is compromised or misconfigured. EKS Auto Mode includes the EKS Pod Identity Agent, so workload identities can be managed through service account to IAM role associations without separately installing the agent.
Rationale: A workload that needs AWS access should run with a dedicated Kubernetes service account associated with an IAM role through EKS Pod Identity, or through IRSA where that model is already in use. With EKS Pod Identity, each Kubernetes service account can be associated with one IAM role in the same AWS account as the cluster, and pods using that service account receive temporary credentials through the EKS Pod Identity Agent and EKS Auth API. The IAM role trust policy uses the pods.eks.amazonaws.com service principal and can be restricted with conditions based on cluster, namespace, and service account context. Using a dedicated service account per workload or permission boundary prevents unrelated pods in the same namespace from sharing the same AWS access. This is stronger than relying on the namespace default service account or reusing one service account across unrelated applications, because only pods explicitly configured to use the associated service account receive the IAM permissions assigned to that role. For IRSA, the same isolation concept applies through an IAM role associated with a Kubernetes service account and the pod’s AWS credential provider chain.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for EKS Auto Mode workloads and map AWS access to those accounts through EKS Pod Identity, or IRSA where required. Create one least privilege IAM role per application or permission boundary, update workloads to reference the intended serviceAccountName, disable token automounting where Kubernetes API access is not needed, and restrict node instance profile access so pods cannot inherit broader node credentials. • Create a dedicated Kubernetes service account for each application or distinct AWS permission boundary instead of sharing the namespace default service account. • Associate that service account with a least privilege IAM role by using EKS Pod Identity where supported, or IRSA where Pod Identity is not supported or not selected. For EKS Pod Identity, create an association between the Kubernetes namespace, service account, and IAM role. The workload manifest must reference that service account for the pod to receive the intended credentials. • Update workload manifests to set spec.serviceAccountName explicitly so the intended service account is always used. • Set automountServiceAccountToken: false for pods or service accounts that do not need Kubernetes API access. • For EKS Pod Identity roles, restrict the trust relationship where appropriate using Pod Identity session tags for cluster, namespace, and service account context. EKS Pod Identity uses the pods.eks.amazonaws.com service principal and supports conditions based on request tags such as Kubernetes namespace and service account.

check.check-content: Review workloads to confirm applications use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts instead of the namespace default service account. Verify the default service account has no workload specific RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings, disable token automounting where Kubernetes API access is not needed, and confirm workloads that need AWS access use the intended IAM role through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA. EKS Auto Mode includes the EKS Pod Identity Agent by default. Review namespace default service accounts and workload manifests to confirm applications use dedicated serviceAccountName values where Kubernetes API or AWS access is required. Confirm the default service account has no workload specific RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings, and set automountServiceAccountToken: false only where the workload does not need Kubernetes API access. Check pods for an explicit service account setting: kubectl get pods -A \ -o custom- columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,SERVICEACCOUNT:.spe c.serviceAccountName,AUTOMOUNT:.spec.automountServiceAccountToken' Check the default service account in each namespace: kubectl get sa -A \ -o custom- columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,AUTOMOUNT:.automou ntServiceAccountToken' | grep ' default ' For any service account that needs closer review, inspect the service account directly and confirm automountServiceAccountToken is set appropriately. For the namespace default service account, a value of false is preferred when workloads do not need Kubernetes API access. kubectl get serviceaccounts/$SERVICE_ACCOUNT \ -n $NAMESPACE \ -o json • Expected output: JSON showing the service account name, namespace, and automountServiceAccountToken settings. Confirm the service account is dedicated to the intended workload and does not automatically mount tokens unless Kubernetes API access is required For workloads that access AWS services, verify the dedicated service account is associated with the intended IAM role through EKS Pod Identity. Where IRSA is still used, confirm the service account annotation and IAM trust policy match the intended namespace, service account, and OIDC provider. Internal Only - General aws eks list-pod-identity-associations \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE • Expected output: a list of Pod Identity associations for the cluster. Review the returned namespace and service account values to confirm expected associations exist. If deeper validation is needed, use the association ID to inspect the IAM role ARN separately.

Group.title: 5.3 KMS Encryption for EKS API Data

Rule.title: Encrypt EKS API data with customer managed KMS keys
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using customer managed KMS keys for EKS envelope encryption adds a customer controlled protection layer for Kubernetes API data stored through the EKS control plane, not only Kubernetes Secrets. This strengthens data at rest protection while allowing organizations to manage key ownership, rotation, policy, and audit visibility for the key used to protect EKS API data. EKS Auto Mode documentation identifies envelope encryption for all Kubernetes API data and AWS KMS integration with either AWS owned keys or customer managed keys.
Rationale: Envelope encryption protects Kubernetes API data stored through the EKS control plane. Plaintext Kubernetes resources are encrypted with data encryption keys before being persisted in etcd, and the data encryption key material is protected with a key encryption key in AWS KMS. This adds a KMS backed encryption layer above the underlying control plane storage encryption and limits plaintext exposure to the Kubernetes API server processing path. In the current EKS model, envelope encryption is enabled by default with an AWS owned key, but a customer managed KMS key can be used when stronger key control, key policy governance, CloudTrail visibility, rotation management, or separation of duties is required. If a customer managed key was previously used for Kubernetes Secrets encryption, that key is also used as the key encryption key for all Kubernetes API data protected by envelope encryption.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Configure the EKS Auto Mode cluster to use a customer managed KMS key for EKS envelope encryption so Kubernetes API data is protected with a customer controlled key encryption key. The key must already exist, be symmetric, support encrypt and decrypt operations, be in the same Region as the cluster, and have permissions that allow EKS to use it. The associate-encryption-config operation does not create a KMS key and does not encrypt arbitrary data directly. It associates an existing customer managed KMS key to the cluster for envelope encryption. In the EKS API, the association is still expressed with resources:["secrets"], but for current EKS envelope encryption, a customer managed key associated for Secrets is used as the key encryption key for Kubernetes API data protected by envelope encryption. Create or identify a customer managed symmetric KMS key that already exists in the same Region as the EKS cluster and is allowed for EKS use. Associate that existing KMS key to the cluster. Replace the variables with real values before running the command. aws eks associate-encryption-config \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --encryption-config "[{\"resources\":[\"secrets\"],\"provider\":{\"keyArn\":\"${KEY_ARN}\"}}]" • Wait for the cluster update to complete, then recheck the cluster configuration and confirm that cluster.encryptionConfig contains resources set to secrets and the expected provider.keyArn. The update runs asynchronously and should be verified before the remediation is considered complete. Keep the associated KMS key enabled and protected from accidental deletion. Do not delete or disable the key while the cluster depends on it, because the cluster can become degraded or unrecoverable if the key is no longer available.

check.check-content: Review the EKS cluster configuration and verify that EKS API data is protected with a customer managed KMS key, not only the default AWS owned envelope encryption key. For this control, the important check is whether the cluster is associated with a customer managed key for EKS envelope encryption. EKS Auto Mode supports envelope encryption for Kubernetes API data using AWS KMS, with options for AWS owned keys or customer managed keys. Review the cluster encryption configuration and confirm a customer managed KMS key ARN is associated with the cluster. If no customer key ARN is associated, the cluster still has default envelope encryption, but it does not meet this customer managed key control. EKS indicates that clusters using a customer managed key show the key ARN, while AWS owned key usage does not expose the key ARN. aws eks describe-cluster \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --query 'cluster.encryptionConfig' • In the command output, verify that the encryption configuration includes resources with secrets and a provider.keyArn value for the customer managed KMS key. Although the API field references secrets, the current EKS envelope encryption model uses the associated customer managed key as the key encryption key for Kubernetes API data protected by envelope encryption. Review the selected KMS key and confirm it is symmetric, supports encrypt and decrypt operations, exists in the same Region as the cluster, and remains enabled. If the key is in another account, confirm the required principal still has access to use it. aws kms describe-key \ --key-id $KEY_ARN \ --region $REGION_CODE • Verify the key policy and grants still allow EKS to use the key. A disabled key, revoked grant, broken key policy, or deleted key can place the cluster into a degraded or unrecoverable state. Where continuous compliance monitoring is used, confirm the cluster would pass the EKS_SECRETS_ENCRYPTED AWS Config rule with the expected customer managed key ARN configured as a parameter. Treat this as a supporting compliance check, while the primary audit evidence remains the EKS cluster encryption configuration and KMS key state. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Enable private EKS API access and restrict public access to approved CIDRs
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This recommendation reduces exposure of the EKS Kubernetes API server endpoint without requiring a private only design. The intended end state is that private endpoint access is enabled, and if the public endpoint remains enabled, public access is restricted to approved CIDR ranges instead of being open to all internet addresses. This preserves approved administration paths while reducing unnecessary internet exposure. EKS supports configuring private access, public access, and public access CIDRs for the Kubernetes API server endpoint.
Rationale: EKS exposes separate endpoint access settings through endpointPrivateAccess, endpointPublicAccess, and publicAccessCidrs. When private access is enabled, Kubernetes API requests from within the cluster VPC use the private VPC endpoint, and access to that private endpoint is controlled by the cluster security group. When public access is enabled, the API server endpoint remains reachable from the internet, but publicAccessCidrs restricts which source ranges can reach the public endpoint. The CIDR allowlist applies only to the public endpoint and does not control the private endpoint. If public access remains enabled, the allowlist should include only trusted administrator, automation, VPN, or network egress CIDR ranges. If private access is not enabled, the public CIDR allowlist must also include the outbound source addresses used by nodes or Fargate pods, such as NAT gateway egress addresses, or those components can lose access to the API server. Enabling private access avoids that dependency for VPC Kubernetes API traffic.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Enable private endpoint access for the EKS Kubernetes API server and restrict public endpoint access to approved CIDR ranges. Private access allows Kubernetes API requests from within the cluster VPC to use the private endpoint. If public access remains enabled, public access CIDRs should be limited to trusted source ranges instead of allowing all internet addresses. If no CIDR blocks are specified, the public endpoint can receive requests from all IP addresses, including 0.0.0.0/0 and, for dual stack clusters,::/0. Internal Only - General Use the following command to enable private access and restrict public access to an approved CIDR. Do not include spaces after the commas in --resources-vpc-config. aws eks update-cluster-config \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --resources-vpc-config endpointPrivateAccess=true,endpointPublicAccess=true,publicAccessCidrs="203.0 .113.5/32" Use the following checks to validate the endpoint access configuration after remediation: • Replace 203.0.113.5/32 with the approved administrator, VPN, automation, or egress CIDR range. • Add only the CIDR ranges required for approved access paths. • After the update completes, rerun the audit command. • Confirm private access is enabled. • Confirm public access is enabled only as intended. • Confirm the public CIDR list does not include unrestricted ranges such as 0.0.0.0/0 or::/0. • Remember that EKS API endpoint access remains a cluster endpoint configuration setting, even when EKS Auto Mode automates other cluster networking functions.

check.check-content: Check that private EKS API endpoint access is enabled, public EKS API endpoint access is enabled only for approved administration paths, and public access CIDRs are restricted to approved source ranges. EKS supports separate settings for private access, public access, and public access CIDRs for the Kubernetes API server endpoint. Public access CIDRs apply only to the public endpoint and do not control the private endpoint. aws eks describe-cluster \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --query "cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.{endpointPrivateAccess:endpointPrivateAccess,endp ointPublicAccess:endpointPublicAccess,publicAccessCidrs:publicAccessCidrs}" \ --output json Expected output: { "endpointPrivateAccess": true, "endpointPublicAccess": true, "publicAccessCidrs": [ "203.0.113.5/32" ] } Look for the following in the output: • Confirm endpointPrivateAccess is set to true. • Confirm endpointPublicAccess is set to true only when public API access is required. • Confirm publicAccessCidrs includes only approved administrator, VPN, automation, or network egress CIDR ranges. • Flag 0.0.0.0/0 as a finding. • For dual stack clusters, also flag::/0 as a finding. • Keep private access enabled when public access is restricted by CIDR, so VPC originated traffic can reach the Kubernetes API server without depending on public endpoint egress paths.

Rule.title: Enable private only EKS API access and disable public endpoint access
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This recommendation is the strict private only version of API endpoint hardening. The intended end state is that the EKS Kubernetes API server endpoint is reachable only from inside the cluster VPC or from a connected private network, and there is no internet reachable public API endpoint. This is a Kubernetes API exposure decision, not an EKS Auto Mode workload networking setting. EKS supports enabling private endpoint access and completely disabling public endpoint access for the Kubernetes API server.
Rationale: In EKS, disabling public access requires private access to be enabled. In that configuration, all traffic to the Kubernetes API server must come from within the cluster VPC or from a connected private network path, and kubectl access from the internet is not available. The private endpoint is controlled by the cluster security group, while publicAccessCidrs becomes irrelevant because there is no public endpoint to filter. The cluster endpoint resolves to private IP addresses for private only access, and administration from outside the VPC must use private connectivity such as VPN, Transit Gateway, Direct Connect, or a managed host inside the VPC.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Enable private endpoint access and disable public endpoint access for the EKS Kubernetes API server. This removes direct internet reachability to the public API endpoint and requires cluster administration through the cluster VPC or a connected private network such as VPN, Transit Gateway, Direct Connect, or an approved management host inside the VPC. EKS allows public and private endpoint access to be configured separately, and the default for new clusters is public access enabled with private access disabled. Before applying this change, confirm that administrators, CI/CD runners, and operational tooling can reach the Kubernetes API through the private access path. aws eks update-cluster-config \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --resources-vpc-config endpointPrivateAccess=true,endpointPublicAccess=false • After the update completes, rerun the audit command and confirm endpointPrivateAccess is true and endpointPublicAccess is false. EKS Auto Mode automates several pod and service networking functions, but Kubernetes API endpoint access remains a cluster endpoint configuration setting.

check.check-content: Verify that the EKS Kubernetes API server endpoint is configured for private only access. Private endpoint access should be enabled, and public endpoint access should be disabled. In this configuration, all traffic to the Kubernetes API server must come from within the cluster VPC or a connected private network. Public access CIDRs are not relevant when public endpoint access is disabled. Internal Only - General aws eks describe-cluster \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --query "cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.{endpointPrivateAccess:endpointPrivateAccess,endp ointPublicAccess:endpointPublicAccess}" \ --output json Expected output: { "endpointPrivateAccess": true, "endpointPublicAccess": false } • Confirm endpointPrivateAccess is true and endpointPublicAccess is false. If public access is still enabled, the cluster does not meet this private only endpoint control. If private access is disabled, do not disable public access until a working VPC or connected private network path is available for administrators and automation.

Rule.title: Deploy EKS Auto Mode nodes only in private subnets
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This recommendation is about the EKS Auto Mode data plane, not the control plane. It means EKS Auto Mode nodes are placed only in private subnets and are not intended to have direct public internet exposure. In the common pattern, nodes run in private subnets while internet facing ingress resources are placed in public subnets. This changes where compute runs and how node traffic exits the VPC, but it does not by itself determine whether the Kubernetes API endpoint is public, private, or both. EKS supports public and private subnets, and private subnets are recommended where possible.
Rationale: EKS Auto Mode supports nodes and pods in public or private subnets, so private subnet placement is a deliberate architecture choice that should be enforced through subnet selection. EKS Auto Mode networking can be customized with a NodeClass, including subnetSelectorTerms, which control how nodes are placed across VPC subnets. A NodeClass can select private subnets by tag or subnet ID, and EKS Auto Mode creates nodes across the matching subnets. Placing EKS Auto Mode nodes in private subnets reduces direct internet reachability of the worker instances and gives tighter control over egress paths. Nodes still need access to required AWS services such as ECR for image pulls, CloudWatch, STS, S3, Elastic Load Balancing, and other services based on workload needs. That access should be provided through NAT gateways, egress only gateways for IPv6, or VPC endpoints where appropriate. In a fully private cluster design with no outbound internet path, private endpoint access and the required VPC endpoints must be planned so nodes and workloads can reach the services they depend on.</VulnDiscussion>
