Rule.fixtext: For EKS Auto Mode nodes placed in public subnets, remediate by updating the NodeClass and NodePool design so Auto Mode provisions nodes only in private subnets. In EKS Auto Mode, subnet placement is controlled through NodeClass subnetSelectorTerms, and NodePools reference the NodeClass that defines the infrastructure configuration. If existing nodes were created from a NodeClass that selects public subnets, create or update a NodeClass that selects only private subnets, then move workloads to NodePools that reference the corrected NodeClass. • Create or update the NodeClass so subnetSelectorTerms selects only private subnet IDs or private subnet tags • Confirm the selected subnets do not auto assign public IPv4 addresses and their route tables do not send 0.0.0.0/0 directly to an Internet Gateway. • If outbound access is required, route it through a NAT gateway, egress only gateway for IPv6, or required VPC endpoints. ECR image pulls from private subnets require NAT or the required ECR and S3 VPC endpoints. • Update or create NodePools that reference the corrected NodeClass, then move workload scheduling to those NodePools. • After workloads are stable, retire any NodePools or NodeClass configurations that still select public subnets. A private subnet design for Auto Mode nodes does not automatically make the EKS API endpoint private. API endpoint access should be evaluated separately through the cluster endpoint access settings.

check.check-content: Review the EKS Auto Mode NodePool and NodeClass configuration to confirm nodes are placed only in private subnets. Validate the NodeClass subnet selection, subnet public IP behavior, and route table design. A compliant design uses subnets that do not auto assign public IPv4 addresses and do not route directly to an Internet Gateway. Review the NodePool and NodeClass configuration and confirm each NodePool references a NodeClass whose subnetSelectorTerms select only private subnets. The NodeClass should use private subnet IDs directly or private subnet tags. kubectl get nodepools,nodeclasses -o yaml • Expected output: JSON showing NodePool and NodeClass configuration. Review each NodePool’s nodeClassRef and confirm the referenced NodeClass subnetSelectorTerms select only private subnet IDs or private subnet tags Resolve the selected subnet IDs from the NodeClass selectors, then verify that those subnets do not auto assign public IPv4 addresses. aws ec2 describe-subnets \ --subnet-ids $SUBNET_IDS \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --query 'Subnets[].{SubnetId:SubnetId,MapPublicIpOnLaunch:MapPublicIpOnLaunch,Tags:Ta gs}' \ --output json • Expected output: JSON showing each subnet ID, whether public IPv4 assignment is enabled, and subnet tags. For private node placement, MapPublicIpOnLaunch should be false for the subnets used by EKS Auto Mode nodes. Verify the route table associated with each node subnet does not contain a default route such as 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway. For IPv6, also verify there is no direct::/0 route to an Internet Gateway unless the design explicitly requires public IPv6 reachability. Private subnets can still have controlled outbound access through NAT, egress only gateways, or VPC endpoints. Note: Confirm outbound dependencies for private nodes are satisfied through NAT gateways, egress only gateways, or VPC endpoints so nodes can pull images, publish logs, and reach required AWS services without direct public exposure. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Use TLS certificates for EKS Auto Mode load balancer listeners
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using TLS certificates on EKS Auto Mode load balancer listeners protects client traffic by presenting a trusted server certificate and negotiating encrypted HTTPS or TLS connections at the listener. In EKS Auto Mode, this commonly means configuring TLS on a Network Load Balancer created from a Kubernetes Service or specifying certificate ARNs for an Application Load Balancer created from IngressClassParams and Ingress resources so externally exposed application entry points do not rely on unencrypted HTTP or TCP traffic. EKS Auto Mode supports load balancing for Kubernetes Services and Ingress resources.
Rationale: EKS Auto Mode supports TLS configuration on both primary load balancer paths. For Network Load Balancers, EKS Auto Mode supports Service annotations such as aws- load-balancer-ssl-cert, which specifies the ACM certificate ARN for HTTPS or TLS, and aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports, which identifies the listener ports that should use SSL or TLS. For Application Load Balancers, EKS Auto Mode uses IngressClassParams, where the certificate to use for SSL or TLS is part of the load balancer configuration. This is important because the listener is the point where the client connection is negotiated, the certificate is presented, and encrypted traffic is established before requests are forwarded to targets. TLS can terminate at the load balancer, at the ingress layer, or continue to the pod depending on the required security model. Requiring certificates on load balancer listeners establishes encrypted external client access, while backend encryption must be handled separately if end to end encryption is required.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Configure every client facing EKS Auto Mode load balancer listener to use HTTPS or TLS with a valid certificate so client to load balancer traffic is encrypted in transit. For NLB backed Service resources, add the ACM certificate ARN and encrypted listener ports in the Service annotations. For ALB backed Ingress resources, configure HTTPS listener behavior through IngressClassParams and associate the required ACM certificate ARN using certificateARNs. If encryption is required beyond the load balancer, implement backend TLS separately because listener TLS alone protects only the client facing connection. • Add a valid ACM certificate to each client facing NLB or ALB listener that should serve encrypted traffic. • For NLB Services, set aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert to the ACM certificate ARN and aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports to the required listener ports. • For ALB Ingress, configure the associated IngressClassParams with certificateARNs for the required HTTPS listener configuration. • Replace, renew, or reassign expired, missing, or mismatched certificates before they affect client access. • Implement backend TLS separately where encryption is required from the load balancer to the backend target. Internal Only - General

check.check-content: Review all client facing EKS Auto Mode load balancers and verify that listeners use HTTPS or TLS with a valid certificate. For NLB backed Service resources, listener TLS is configured with annotations such as aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert for the ACM certificate ARN and aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports for the encrypted listener ports. For ALB backed Ingress resources, the certificate is configured through IngressClassParams using certificateARNs. A TCP listener on port 443 may pass encrypted traffic through, but it should be documented separately because it does not terminate TLS at the load balancer. • Identify all internet facing or client facing Service resources of type LoadBalancer and all Ingress resources. • Verify NLB backed Services use aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert and aws- load-balancer-ssl-ports when TLS is intended to terminate at the NLB. • Verify ALB backed Ingress configurations use IngressClassParams with certificateARNs for HTTPS listeners. • Verify the ACM certificate covers the intended hostname and is valid for the listener configuration. • Verify the listener design matches the intended TLS termination point. TLS may terminate at the load balancer, ingress layer, or continue to the pod depending on the required security model.

Rule.title: Use EKS access entries for IAM principal Kubernetes access
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using EKS access entries centralizes how IAM principals are granted access to the Kubernetes API and lets cluster access be managed through Amazon EKS instead of relying on manual aws-auth ConfigMap updates. This gives a cleaner access management model for users and roles that need to work with Kubernetes resources in the cluster. For EKS Auto Mode, access entries are especially important because Kubernetes API access is secured through EKS access entries integrated with IAM identities, and access entries cannot be disabled on an EKS Auto Mode cluster.
Rationale: An access entry associates an IAM principal, such as an IAM role or IAM user, with Kubernetes permissions in the cluster. For EKS Auto Mode, the cluster authentication mode must include the EKS API because Auto Mode requires EKS access entries. The aws-auth ConfigMap can be enabled as an optional compatibility path, but it should not remain the primary model for routine IAM principal access. Permissions can be granted by associating EKS access policies to the access entry, or by mapping the principal to Kubernetes groups and continuing authorization through Kubernetes RBAC objects such as Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, and ClusterRoleBindings. EKS access policies can be applied cluster or limited to specific namespaces, while Kubernetes group mappings are better suited when highly customized RBAC is required. This allows standard access to be managed through EKS APIs while preserving Kubernetes RBAC for more specialized permission models.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:subject: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Configure the cluster to use EKS access entries for IAM principal access management, then create and scope access entries for each required IAM role or user. For EKS Auto Mode, access entries should be the primary access model because Auto Mode uses access entries and they cannot be disabled. This remediation typically starts by enabling the access entry API through the cluster authentication mode, then moving existing access management from legacy aws-auth ConfigMap mappings to access entries with EKS access policies, Kubernetes RBAC group mappings, or both. Moving from CONFIG_MAP to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP is the recommended transition path when legacy mappings still need to be preserved during migration. Update the cluster authentication mode to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP. aws eks update-cluster-config \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --access-config authenticationMode=API_AND_CONFIG_MAP Create an access entry for each IAM principal that needs Kubernetes access. Each access entry maps one existing IAM role or IAM user to cluster access. aws eks create-access-entry \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --principal-arn $PRINCIPAL_ARN \ --region $REGION_CODE Associate the required EKS access policies to the access entry, or map the principal to Kubernetes groups and authorize it through RBAC objects such as Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, and ClusterRoleBindings. Scope access to specific namespaces where possible. aws eks associate-access-policy \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --principal-arn $PRINCIPAL_ARN \ --policy-arn $ACCESS_POLICY_ARN \ --access-scope type=namespace,namespaces=$NAMESPACE \ --region $REGION_CODE • Use cluster access only where it is required. For application teams or namespace limited operators, prefer namespace access scopes or Kubernetes RBAC group mappings instead of broad cluster permissions.

check.check-content: Review the cluster access model and verify IAM principal access to Kubernetes is managed through EKS access entries rather than relying only on legacy aws-auth ConfigMap mappings. For EKS Auto Mode, access entries are required and cannot be disabled, although the aws-auth ConfigMap can optionally remain enabled for compatibility. Access entries are available only when the cluster authentication mode is set to API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, and permissions can be granted through EKS access policies, Kubernetes groups for RBAC, or both. Verify the cluster authentication mode is API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP. aws eks describe-cluster \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE \ --query 'cluster.accessConfig.authenticationMode' \ --output text • Expected output: API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP Note: If the output is CONFIG_MAP, the cluster does not satisfy this audit step. Review the cluster’s access entries and confirm each required IAM role or user has an access entry, with no duplicate, unused, or unnecessary principals. aws eks list-access-entries \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --region $REGION_CODE Review each access entry and confirm the principal ARN, Kubernetes groups, and entry type match the intended access model. aws eks describe-access-entry \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --principal-arn $PRINCIPAL_ARN \ --region $REGION_CODE Review the permissions attached to each access entry and confirm they are granted through the intended EKS access policies, Kubernetes groups, or both, with access limited to the required namespace or cluster level. aws eks list-associated-access-policies \ --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --principal-arn $PRINCIPAL_ARN \ --region $REGION_CODE • Expected output: Associated access policies for the selected IAM principal. Review the policy ARN and access scope to confirm permissions are limited to the intended cluster or namespaces. EKS access policies can be associated with access entries, while Kubernetes group mappings can continue to use Kubernetes RBAC for custom permission models. Internal Only - General Review any remaining aws-auth ConfigMap usage and flag legacy mappings that should be migrated or removed if access entries are now the intended management path. After access entries are created for existing aws-auth mappings, the old ConfigMap entries can be removed where they are no longer needed.
